name: Sitting height ratio

card.summary: A measurement of torso length against total height (the inverse view of leg-to-torso proportion) that people use to understand how long their legs look and which clothing and fit choices flatter their frame.
card.aka: Cormic index, leg-to-torso ratio, sitting body ratio

quick.overview:
Sitting height ratio is sitting height divided by standing height, multiplied by 100. Because sitting height covers the head and trunk, a lower ratio means proportionally longer legs, and a higher ratio means a proportionally longer torso. In looksmaxxing circles it is used to describe body proportions: people with long legs relative to torso are often said to look taller and more athletic.

Body-proportion researchers use the same measure as a marker of growth conditions in childhood and as a variable in studies of health, and one review includes a note on its link to perceived beauty. Wikipedia reports attractiveness ratings that favour a roughly 1:2 leg-to-body ratio in men.
quick.how: People measure it at home with a wall, a flat chair or bench and a tape: standing height, then height while seated upright with the back against the wall, and divide. Once they know their proportions, many use the result to choose clothing cuts, trouser rises, shoe styles and posture or training emphases that balance the frame (for example high-rise trousers and tucked tops to visually lengthen legs).
quick.risks: The measurement itself carries no risk. The main caution raised by researchers is interpretive: leg length estimated from sitting height can be biased by body fat, and population averages differ, so a single number does not map neatly onto how someone looks.

lead: Sitting height ratio (SHR), also called the cormic index, is sitting height divided by standing height, expressed as a percentage. Because sitting height includes the head and trunk, the remainder of stature is mostly leg length, so a lower SHR corresponds to relatively longer legs and a higher SHR to a relatively longer trunk [1][2].

Within looksmaxxing, the ratio is one of the ways people describe body proportions alongside shoulder-to-waist ratio and height. Those with proportionally long legs are commonly described as looking taller than their measured height, and people use their own ratio to guide clothing fit, shoe choice and styling that balances their frame. A body-proportions summary on Wikipedia notes that leg length relative to body length is treated as an indicator of physical attractiveness, while stating there is no single accepted definition of leg length [8].

Research on the measure comes mostly from human biology and epidemiology. Reviews describe it as a marker of environmental quality during childhood growth and as a variable associated with later health outcomes, and one review carries a short note on beauty [1][2].

chain: Measure sitting height against standing height
Learn whether legs or torso are proportionally long
Choose cuts, rises and shoes that balance the frame
angle.text: Knowing the ratio tells someone where their proportions sit relative to the average, which they use to pick clothing silhouettes and footwear that make legs look longer or torso look more balanced. The ratio itself is a descriptor; the styling choices are what change the look.

paras: Sitting height is measured with the person seated upright on a flat surface, from the surface to the top of the head. Dividing by standing height and multiplying by 100 gives the ratio. Subtracting sitting height from stature gives an estimate of leg length (subischial length) [1][8].

The Wikipedia article on body proportions describes a closely related sitting body ratio in which the trunk is measured on a flat chair or table and leg length is found by subtraction, and notes that this nearly matches the perineum-to-floor measure while avoiding touching an intimate area [8].
Reviews describe a cephalo-caudal growth gradient: between birth and puberty the legs grow relatively faster than the rest of the body, so children's ratio falls as they grow [1][2].

Researchers have used SHR as an indicator of the environment for growth. A review states that, for groups of children, short stature with relatively short legs (a high ratio) generally marks an adverse growth environment [1]. In a study of Maya children, those raised in the United States were on average 10.24 cm taller and had relatively longer legs than Maya children in Guatemala, which the authors attributed to better nutrition and health [3].

The same reviews note that the development of proportions reflects gene and environment interactions, with few specific genes known [1]. A genome-wide analysis of body proportion has examined height-associated variants by their effect on skeletal proportions [7].

A study of NHANES III data reported that body fatness biases the use of estimated leg length as an epidemiological marker in adults [4]. A separate paper found that secular changes in relative leg length affect height-based reference values for lung function [5]. These issues concern research use of the ratio, but they also show why individual values are best read as approximate descriptors.

In appearance discussions the ratio is used to describe whether someone has a long torso or long legs. People with a high ratio often look to styling: high-rise trousers, shorter tops, shoes with a continuous line from trouser to shoe, and lifts or posture work to add apparent height. Those with a low ratio sometimes describe wanting to balance a tall, leggy frame with torso-building training. These are community practices rather than prescriptions from the research literature.

Human studies treat SHR as an anthropometric variable. Reviews link relative leg length with epidemiological risk markers such as overweight, coronary heart disease and diabetes, and with the quality of the growth environment in childhood [1][2]. One review proposes assessing mothers' sitting height ratio as an indicator of their early-life nutrition when studying later obesity [6]. These studies describe population patterns; none tests changing the ratio for appearance.
